---
title: "The AI Divide: The Equity Problem We Can't Afford to Ignore"
---

*An opinion piece by Michael Borck*

---

Higher education is currently talking about how AI will transform assessment, pedagogy, and the student experience. That conversation matters, and it has a blind spot.

The divide is already here. It operates at two levels: the student in your classroom, and the institution that classroom sits within.

## The Student-Level Divide

In any given tutorial, some students walk in with GPT-4, Claude, Gemini Advanced, and a suite of frontier AI tools. Others are working with whatever free tier they can get on a phone with a cracked screen and a prepaid data plan.

This is not a hypothetical case; it happens in ordinary tutorials.

Students who can afford $20-30 USD per month for a frontier model subscription work with fundamentally different cognitive tools than those who can't. They get better feedback on writing, more sophisticated help with problems, and stronger research support. The gap between free and paid AI keeps widening.

AI is often described as a great equaliser. We should stop describing it that way. It currently acts as a great *amplifier*, of advantage for those who have it and of disadvantage for those who don't.

## The Institutional Divide

At the institutional level, a second fracture appears.

Perkins and Roe (2025) get this right: the traditional Global North/South framing misses the point. The determinants are structural: connectivity, computing power, capacity to train staff, and depth of AI literacy. Here in Australia, a sandstone university in Sydney with a dedicated AI strategy unit works in different conditions from a regional provider in the Northern Territory, where reliable broadband is still a challenge. The divide runs through a single country, let alone across the globe.

One statistic captures the problem: the data needed to build cutting-edge GenAI models exists for roughly one per cent of the world's languages. As Perkins and Roe put it, the framing of AI as the great democratiser of education is "more myth than reality."

Well-resourced institutions are already piloting AI-embedded assessment, portfolio-based evaluation, and authentic collaborative tasks. They have room to experiment and iterate.

Under-resourced institutions face a different calculus. When funding is thin and any misstep invites scrutiny, innovation looks like risk. The rational response is retrenchment: more invigilated exams, tighter lockdown browsers, and heavier penalties for AI use. These are assessment practices that predate electricity, let alone artificial intelligence.

The distance between the two grows every semester, along fault lines of funding, geography, and structural advantage that were entrenched long before ChatGPT.

## We've Seen This Before

We saw it with the internet, with learning management systems, and with COVID and online learning. The same script ran each time: early adoption by the well-resourced, a defensive reaction by the under-resourced, and a widening gap dressed up as "digital transformation."

The difference this time is speed. Previous cycles gave institutions years to catch up. AI capabilities advance quarterly and pedagogical implications shift monthly. Standing still means falling behind faster.

## What Needs to Change

Any framework for AI in education must address power, bias, and access alongside capability (Roe, Furze & Perkins, 2025). The assessment conversation needs that same lens.

In practice:

1. Institutions must provide AI access. If AI is integral to how we teach and assess, equitable access is an institutional responsibility. We already provide library access and software licences. AI access should be no different.

2. Invest in under-resourced institutions as a priority. The institutions that need the most support are the least likely to develop it internally.

3. Design for resource diversity. Assessment that only works when students have frontier model access, or when institutions can invest in sophisticated AI platforms, is a privilege.

4. Centre the voices on the wrong side of this divide. Right now, the conversation about AI in education is dominated by those with the most resources. The people most affected are the least represented.

## The Stakes

The promise of AI in education is real: personalised learning, immediate feedback, more authentic assessment. These will remain fantasies for most of the world's learners unless we confront the equity dimension directly.

The AI divide is the central issue. Every conversation about AI in education needs to start with a simple question: who gets left behind?

If we can't answer that honestly, we are not transforming education; we are only making inequality faster.
